normalization.title: When Code Gets Cheap, Ambition Becomes the Test
normalization.overview: Suhail Doshi argues cheap models, always-on agents and code-native work expand what people can build. The economic, engineering and human acceptance limits matter more than a headline price ratio.
normalization.whyItMatters: Falling implementation costs are changing the feasibility of work while moving scarcity into evaluation, state, safety, permission and problem selection.
normalization.ghostMeshTakeaway: Measure cost per accepted result, build enforceable agent-native interfaces, and scale ambitions only with source provenance, bounded authority and recoverable state.

archiveCall.label: Test feasible work, not token prices
archiveCall.text: Use representative paired workloads, real acceptance receipts, human review time, tool spend and rollback tests before choosing a premium or inexpensive model.

normalization.falsification: Run representative paired tasks across premium, cheaper and routed models; blind scoring where feasible; track all retries, accepted outputs, human verification, latency, safety, version custody and total cost; test expanded scope separately.
normalization.freshness: Original interview Nov 21, Particle Oct 28, Stanford 2025, METR Feb 2026. Analysis as of Nov 22, 2026; predictions and vendor claims not independently replicated.

claims.proposition: Long-horizon and always-on agents may increase aggregate consumption despite lower token prices
claims.assessment: Doshi observes longer trajectories and proposes 24/7 agents; no measured adoption/cost forecast in source.
claims.limits: Not an observed 24/7 agent fleet or aggregate demand forecast.

claims.proposition: Benchmark-normalized inference prices declined sharply in 2022–24
claims.sourceLocation: Stanford AI Index 2025, Research and Development chapter, numbered highlight 6 (plus Stanford ten-chart summary); interview 09:15 merely contextual
claims.assessment: Stanford HAI documents >280x price reduction at fixed MMLU threshold through Oct 2024. Source: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/research-and-development. The video price discussion is context, not the numerical report origin. Exact numbers are stated in chapter highlight 6: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/research-and-development and in Stanford HAI official 10-chart summary: https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-index-2025-state-of-ai-in-10-charts.
claims.limits: Historical benchmark-matched comparison does not prove frontier price declines for all task types.

claims.proposition: Particle-1 token efficiency improves under vendor software/data benchmark
claims.assessment: Particle Oct 28 reports 28.4-52.2% fewer output tokens, 34.4-51.6% lower cost per task than base DeepSeek V4.1 Flash across four benchmarks, pass@1 within confidence intervals. Vendor cost calculation assumes 95% cache hit and counts failed attempts; it is not audited cost per independently accepted real-world job.
claims.limits: Vendor study; fixed price/cache assumptions; no independent replication; distinguish compression from omission of needed checks. Reported average task cost includes failures and fixed cache conditions, not full human acceptance, correction and recovery.

claims.proposition: Interview describes a 30× subjective design price comparison and a separate Fable quality estimate, not one matched trial
claims.assessment: At https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2UEMxBTu9M&t=1901s Doshi informally compares premium GPT-family output and DeepSeek Flash design results, with approximately 30x different model pricing. At https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2UEMxBTu9M&t=1912s he separately offers a subjective 10–20% Fable improvement estimate. The automatic caption aid does not certify the exact premium GPT model identity.
claims.limits: Not a single paired Fable-vs-DeepSeek evaluation; no pinned sample, independent blind scoring, repeated runs or audited model prices.

claims.proposition: Five personally chosen tasks provide a useful switching signal
claims.assessment: Doshi recommends a small repeatable task folder, common prompts, and scoring, useful as a pilot.
claims.limits: Five prompts are not representative/statistically robust; grader/model preferences and task selection bias.

claims.proposition: Video/doc/3D workflows may favor direct code/FFmpeg/Blender APIs over visual-app control
claims.assessment: Riley reports direct FFmpeg workflow works better in his creative setup; Doshi suggests training distribution explanation.
claims.limits: Not a controlled latency, correctness, usability or total-cost comparison; file/asset custody risks remain.

claims.proposition: Headless agents can obscure intermediate files and authoritative versions
claims.assessment: Riley reports users losing track of produced files and versions; Doshi forecasts model-mediated version retention.
claims.limits: A prediction of improved agents is not a durable store, access policy or rollback receipt.

claims.proposition: AI-native engineering changes task boundaries and career opportunities
claims.assessment: Doshi argues software engineers increasingly build AI systems and may have to re-skill; claims are rhetorical.
claims.limits: Not evidence the profession is extinct; productivity varies and hiring impacts require separate evidence.

claims.proposition: AI coding productivity is mixed and context-dependent in existing independent studies
claims.sourceLocation: METR 2025 experiment and Feb 2026 follow-up; interview 43:25 contextual
claims.assessment: METR early-2025 observed 19% longer completion time on specified tasks; Feb 2026 followup says selection effects weaken numerical inference for more recent periods. Primary reports: https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/ and https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/. The video career discussion is not the source of the measured percentages.
claims.limits: Limited participant/task selection; cannot generalize to all workers.

claims.proposition: Recreating GTA 1 to GTA VI is a proposed composite evaluation
claims.assessment: Doshi suggests a progressively difficult game recreation benchmark; interview reports no execution.
claims.limits: No defined acceptance, rights-cleared assets, pass-rate or cost.

claims.proposition: Cheaper code and code-native interfaces could expand feasible creative project scope
claims.assessment: The interview argues for scaling individual ambition and structural room to attempt larger projects.
claims.limits: No causal data on labor opportunity, income, ownership or long-term project outcomes.

claims.proposition: More creative access to robotics may follow from programmable agents
claims.assessment: Interview extrapolates from recent arm demos to more broad access, not empirical robot deployment.
claims.limits: No repeatability, held-out testing, sim-to-real verification or safety assurance.

claims.proposition: Particle earns token revenue while aiming to lower token price
claims.assessment: Founder describes the apparent margin/volume tension and compares inference to payments; underdetermined economics.
claims.limits: No audited financials, future scale economics, or provider cost breakdown.

relationships.reason: Reader #69 develops accepted-work cost accounting beyond token price. It is a complementary economic lens, not evidence that the interview forecasts are correct.
Reader #70 shows how specific workload evaluation limits general model-price comparisons. It is methodological background, not independent validation of Particle-1.

sharePlaneRelationships.title: The Right Model Is the One Your Eval Can Defend
sharePlaneRelationships.reason: A publicly published evaluation playbook for representative task samples, trace-level errors, model baselines and operating cost. It supplies a concrete qualification approach but not empirical evidence for Doshi.

sharePlaneRelationships.title: The Best AI System Should Need Less AI Tomorrow
sharePlaneRelationships.reason: The published inference-retirement thesis asks what should become deterministic after validation. It extends the architecture/control side of cheap model tokens without verifying the video claims.

normalization.relationshipDisposition: Two relevant published Readers (#69 cost accounting, #70 workload-specific model evaluation), two published conceptual SharePlane Works; none independently corroborates the interview.
